newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel mulls change to exchange regime.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel mulls change to exchange regime.

text.p: The Bank of Israel is studying a possible change to the foreign exchange regime which would lead to a slower pace in the Israeli shekel's annual rate of depreciation, central bank sources said over the weekend.
The shekel is pegged to a basket of foreign currencies and can trade in a band of seven percent above or below a sloping midpoint which rises six percent a year.
Some senior economists in the central bank support reducing the rate of increase in the slope to four percent a year from six percent, the sources said.
The depreciation rate, which has not changed since 1993, reflects the difference between Israeli inflation and inflation among Israel's main trading partners.

Bank of Israel economists noted that the government's 1997 inflation target is seven to 10 percent, or an average of 8.5 percent. Since inflation in Israel's main trading partners averages 4.5 percent, some Bank of Israel officials believe the shekel's depreciation rate should be four percent rather than six percent.
Central bank officials believe the issue should be raised later this year during discussions to set the 1998 inflation target.
A slower rate of depreciation would require less intervention on the part of the central bank to prevent the shekel from appreciating beyond its trading band.
The central bank has been required to buy large amounts of foreign currency in the past year to prevent the shekel from appreciating beyond its band. In 1997 alone the central bank bought $5 billion.

Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel called for a widening of the trading band to avoid such a massive intervention, but the Treasury was opposed, arguing this would lead to the shekel's appreciation.
